r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
d=Path('tmp/pdfs')

parts=[]

    t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    (d/f'page-{i}.txt').write_text(t)
    parts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+t)
(d/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for brain-to-text NLP: evaluation protocols can obscure whether models generalize to unseen subjects and unseen linguistic stimuli.

The proposed requirement to separate both subjects and stimuli is appropriate for jointly testing these generalization capabilities. The discussion of overlapping fMRI windows identifies an additional dependency that naive sample splitting can miss.

Experiments cover two public datasets, EEG and fMRI, two established decoding models, and several splitting and training configurations. This provides useful breadth for investigating evaluation sensitivity.
weaknesses: The published algorithms do not enforce the central zero-leakage guarantee. Algorithm 1, lines 13–16, restores edges for training subjects without excluding held-out text nodes, potentially reintroducing text overlap. Algorithm 2, lines 31–34, checks task membership without excluding held-out subjects. Appendix B also describes splitting fMRI data by subjects, whereas Algorithm 2 specifies tasks. These inconsistencies must be resolved and the resulting partitions independently verified.

The reported metrics require an audit. In Table 4, EEG2Text has ROUGE-1 recall 23.98, precision 23.95, and F-score 25.74; this is impossible under standard, consistently aggregated F1 scoring. Similar inconsistencies occur repeatedly in Table 3. Equation 8 also measures intersection of individual signals although the stated concern is shared subject identity; disjoint recordings from the same subject need not intersect. Thus the numerical evidence cannot presently be accepted without clarification and correction.

Section 5.2 does not establish the claimed causal effects of leakage. Decreasing validation loss or increasing evaluation scores with training are not themselves evidence of leakage or overfitting. Comparisons also change subject/text distributions and potentially retained data volume; Table 2 additionally changes initialization, learning rate, and training duration. Controlled comparisons using a common uncontaminated test set and matched training budgets are needed. Language-only and shuffled-signal controls would directly test the proposed memorization mechanism; random encoder initialization is not a no-signal control.

The claim that all previous splitting methods suffer from leakage overgeneralizes across different evaluation objectives. Decoding unseen text from previously observed subjects is a legitimate within-subject task. The proposed protocol evaluates joint subject-and-stimulus generalization, and conclusions about invalid prior estimates should be restricted to studies claiming that capability.

The benchmark is insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Although Section 5.3 states that it is released, the manuscript provides no access information or exact split manifests. Post-filtering sample counts, retained subjects and stimuli per partition, generation settings, and whether evaluation uses free-running decoding rather than gold prefixes are unclear. Four seeds are reported for leakage measurements, but variability across training runs and benchmark partitions is not reported.

The stated dataset-utilization and generalization benefits are not demonstrated. There are no retained/discarded-data counts or comparisons with straightforward disjoint subject-and-stimulus partitioning. A stricter evaluation split measures generalization; it does not by itself improve it. The useful evaluation objective could support a contribution, but the algorithmic inconsistencies and unreliable evaluation evidence require correction and controlled reevaluation before a Findings recommendation.
